lines.text: Now I had the real question. Why did a UI change cause a support spike? I needed to see it.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: And I had seven minutes with Priya tomorrow. Whatever I brought her had to hold up.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I pinged Kenji, our analyst. Asked for the chart, the stat, and a one-paragraph summary.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Hour later, he sends me the whole bundle. Looked ready to ship. But I'd learned to check before I trust.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: First thing — the chart. Cancel tickets versus the UI ship date.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: What does your eye tell you? Huge spike, right? Looks like a cliff.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Now look at the actual numbers. About fifty thousand, up to fifty-three thousand. That's a six-percent bump.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: The chart made a six-percent change look like a doubling. Priya would've spotted that in two seconds.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: The name for this is a truncated axis. Forget the name. Remember the test. When your eye says one thing, and the numbers say another — something's off.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Next — Kenji's headline claim. UI change drove a forty-seven percent increase. P less than point oh five.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Sounds definitive. But how much data did he actually look at?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Three weeks.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Think about it. Kenji's making a claim about millions of Uber riders, over the long run. With three weeks of post-ship data. It's like polling ten people and making a claim about a whole country.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Analysts call this sample size. The test is simpler — does the size of the data match the size of the claim you're making?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Third piece — Kenji's summary paragraph. Listen.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Analysis indicates a statistically significant correlation between the December 14 deployment and a substantial increase in rider support engagement.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Sounds polished. But if Priya asked me — what's he recommending? — I couldn't tell her. It doesn't commit.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: A real version: Revert the December 14 Cancel button change. Projected thirty-five percent ticket reduction. Forty engineering hours. Priya can sign that in thirty seconds.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: This stuff — text that sounds smart but doesn't commit — we call it slop. Especially common now, because AI makes it easy to write. Test — can the reader do something with it?
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Three forms. Same question underneath.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Chart — does the visual match the numbers? Stat — does the data match the claim? Prose — can the reader act on it? When any of those break — it's slop.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: I sent it back. Kenji rebuilt it.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Chart honest from zero. Claim scaled to what we actually know. Prose committing to one recommendation. Still makes the case — now it holds up.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: At Airbnb, someone will hand you a chart, a stat, and a summary. Don't nod.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Visual against numbers. Data against claim. Prose against action. Those are the three checks. Every time.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Your turn.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Four situations. For each — tell me if the evidence holds up.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Nice. Now — here's a real one.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: A PM just sent you a product recommendation deck. Chart, stat, summary — the whole package.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Before it goes up the chain — stress-test it with Claude. I'll walk you through how to ask.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: First — try asking Claude your own way. Whatever feels natural.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: See how vague your question got you a vague answer? Let me teach you the sharp ones.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Always put your claim in the question. What am I trying to say? What decision is someone making? Then ask Claude if the evidence actually holds.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Copy these questions. They're your toolkit. When you're done — send the fixed bundle back to me.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: That's the move. You didn't need a statistics degree. You needed four questions.
lines.speaker: avery

lines.text: Honest chart. Real finding. Next — how do you turn it into something someone can actually act on?
lines.speaker: avery
